p: The written Hebrew has 'your feet'; the Masoretes' reading tradition has 'your foot'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv); the Syriac Peshitta agrees
readings.plain: Keep watch over your feet

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere), as vocalized in the codex; Greek (Rahlfs) τὸν πόδα σου; KJV
readings.plain: Keep watch over your foot

why: The meaning is the same. The Plain follows the written text because 'your feet' is natural English for how a person walks; the KJV and the Greek have the singular.

a: Coming close to listen is better than giving a sacrifice the way fools do
t: Better than fools' sacrifice, or your sacrifice better?
p: The Greek and Syriac read 'your sacrifice is better than the gift of fools'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum
readings.en: and drawing near to listen, more than fools' giving of a sacrifice
readings.plain: Coming close to listen is better than giving a sacrifice the way fools do

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs); Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees; the Syriac Peshitta is close ('better than the gift of fools' sacrifices')
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγγὺς τοῦ ἀκούειν· ὑπὲρ δόμα τῶν ἀφρόνων θυσία σου
readings.en: and be near to listen; your sacrifice is better than the gift of fools
readings.plain: Come close to listen. Your sacrifice is better than the gift of fools

why: The Hebrew makes good sense and fits the prophets' 'listening is better than sacrifice'. The Greek read the same consonants but took 'giving' (mittet) as a noun, 'gift' (mattat), and added 'your'.

t: Before the messenger, or before God?
p: The Hebrew has 'the messenger' (or angel); the Greek and the Syriac have 'God'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum ('the cruel angel')
readings.plain: before the messenger

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: before God

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading: a scribe or translator is more likely to change an unclear 'messenger' into 'God' than the reverse. The Greek may also be harmonizing with 'before God' in 5:2. Most modern translations follow the Hebrew.
b: No Dead Sea Scroll preserves this verse. The note at 5:6 gives the readings of 'the messenger'.

p: The Greek read the same Hebrew letters as 'slave'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Syriac Peshitta; Targum ('a man who serves the Lord')
readings.en: the worker (one who works the ground)
readings.plain: A worker's sleep

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees)
readings.plain: A slave's sleep

why: The consonants 'bd can be read 'oved, 'worker', or 'eved, 'slave'. The Masoretic vowels give 'worker', which fits the contrast with the rich man. The Greek reading is a different vocalization, not a different text.

a: he eats in darkness all his days, and he is greatly frustrated
t: He eats in darkness, or his days are darkness and mourning?
p: The Greek reads 'and mourning' where the Hebrew has 'he eats', and the scroll 4QQoh-a has neither.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Syriac Peshitta (which also adds 'and in mourning'); Targum
readings.orig: גַּם כָּל־יָמָיו בַּחֹשֶׁךְ יֹאכֵל וְכָעַס הַרְבֵּה
readings.en: also all his days in darkness he eats, and he is very vexed
readings.plain: he eats in darkness all his days, and he is greatly frustrated

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees)
readings.orig: καί γε πᾶσαι αἱ ἡμέραι αὐτοῦ ἐν σκότει καὶ πένθει καὶ θυμῷ πολλῷ
readings.en: and all his days are in darkness and mourning and much anger
readings.plain: all his days are in darkness and mourning, with much frustration

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QQoh-a (4Q109, copied about the middle of the 100s BC), in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription
readings.en: also all his days in darkness, vexation much
readings.plain: all his days are in darkness, with much frustration

why: The Leningrad Codex is followed, but this is a close call. The Greek seems to have read ve'evel, 'and mourning', for yokhel, 'he eats', two words that look alike in Hebrew script, and many scholars (for example Seow and Fox) prefer it. The oldest witness, 4QQoh-a, has no verb at all, which may support a text without 'he eats'.
b: The scroll's word for 'vexation' lacks the 'and' of the Leningrad Codex, so in the scroll it is a noun ('much frustration'), not a verb. Words in brackets are restored by the editors.

a: is to be in silver's shade
t: In the shade, or like the shade?
p: The Hebrew repeats 'in the shade'; the Greek and Syriac compare wisdom's shade to money's.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: in the shade of the silver
readings.plain: is to be in silver's shade

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs: ὡς σκιὰ τοῦ ἀργυρίου); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: is like being in silver's shade

why: The Hebrew letters b ('in') and k ('like') look alike, and the Greek and Syriac may have read k. Both readings give the same sense: wisdom protects as money does. The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex.

a: Wisdom does more to make the wise strong
p: The Hebrew has 'makes strong'; the oldest scroll, the Greek and the Syriac have 'helps'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum
readings.plain: Wisdom does more to make the wise strong

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QQoh-a (4Q109), in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription; Greek (Rahlfs: βοηθήσει); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: Wisdom does more to help the wise

why: The two Hebrew verbs, ta'oz 'makes strong' and ta'zor 'helps', differ by one letter. The scroll, the Greek and the Syriac agree on 'helps', which is strong evidence that it is old; some scholars prefer it. The Leningrad reading is also good Hebrew and fits 'more than ten rulers'. The sense hardly changes.

t: Says Qohelet, or says the Qohelet?
p: The Leningrad Codex has a feminine verb. Divided differently, the same letters say 'says the Qohelet', as in 12:8.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum
readings.plain: says Qohelet

readings.w: The same consonants divided as in 12:8 (amar haqqohelet), proposed by most modern scholars; Greek (Rahlfs: εἶπεν ὁ Ἐκκλησιαστής, with the article) and Syriac Peshitta read a masculine verb
readings.plain: says the Qohelet

why: Moving one letter from the end of the verb to the start of the name gives the form found in 12:8, with a masculine verb and 'the' before Qohelet. The Greek, with the article, supports this. The meaning is unchanged except that 'the Qohelet' sounds like a title. The Plain keeps the name without 'the', as in 1:1–2 and 12:8–10.

a: Who is like the wise man?
t: Who is like the wise, or who knows the wise?
p: The Greek reads 'Who knows the wise?'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Syriac Peshitta; Targum
readings.en: who is like the wise man?
readings.plain: Who is like the wise man?

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees)
readings.plain: Who knows the wise?

why: The Hebrew form kehechakham is unusual (the 'h' of 'the' is normally swallowed after k), which may have led the Greek to read the line differently. The Syriac and the Targum support the Hebrew.

a: and the stern look on his face is changed
p: The Greek and Syriac read 'the bold of face will be hated'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum
readings.en: and the strength of his face is changed
readings.plain: and the stern look on his face is changed

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs: ἀναιδὴς προσώπῳ αὐτοῦ μισηθήσεται); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: and the one with a hard face will be hated

why: The Hebrew yeshunne' 'is changed' is written with a final aleph, as if from a verb 'to hate' (sane'); the Greek and Syriac read it that way. The Masoretic reading fits the parallel with a face that shines.

a: I say, do what the king's mouth tells you
p: The Hebrew begins with 'I'. The Greek and the Syriac have no 'I'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I: the mouth of a king keep
readings.plain: I say, do what the king's mouth tells you

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs: στόμα βασιλέως φύλαξον); Syriac Peshitta
readings.en: keep the mouth of a king
readings.plain: Do what the king's mouth tells you

why: The bare 'I' is awkward, and some scholars think it began as the object marker 'et or that a verb like 'I say' has dropped out. The Plain keeps it and supplies 'say', as the KJV does ('I counsel thee').

p: Most Hebrew manuscripts read 'forgotten'. The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts read 'praised'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Syriac Peshitta; Targum; KJV
readings.plain: they were forgotten

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs: ἐπῃνέθησαν; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees); some medieval Hebrew manuscripts, as reported in the critical editions; the Talmud's reading 'do not read ... but praised' (Gittin 56b); many modern translations
readings.plain: they were praised

why: The two Hebrew words differ by one letter (k or b), which look alike. 'Praised' makes the verse a complaint: the wicked are honored in the city where they did wrong, which is why it is vapor. 'Forgotten' can also work if the subject is those who had done right (see the note). The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex, with the Syriac and Targum; the case for 'praised' is strong.

t: A hundred times, or from then on?
p: The Hebrew has an odd spelling of 'a hundred'. The Greek read 'from then on'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and most modern versions
readings.plain: a hundred times

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs: ἀπὸ τότε; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees)
readings.plain: from then on

why: Me'at is an unusual spelling of me'ah, 'a hundred', but 'a hundred' gives good sense: however often the sinner does evil, he still lives long. The Greek seems to have read me'az, 'from then', a word that differs in its last letter. Most translations follow the Hebrew.
b: With 'a hundred' the verse sets the sinner's hundred wrongs against his long life, which is the point of 8:12–14. No Dead Sea Scroll preserves this verse.
